lines: Your first job offer pays 55,000 dollars a year. How much of that goes to federal income tax? Less than most people think, because income tax is figured in layers.
First, the standard deduction. In 2026, the first 16,100 dollars a single person earns isn't taxed. 55,000 minus 16,100 leaves 38,900 dollars of taxable income.
Next, the brackets. Picture buckets. Your dollars fill the 10 percent bucket first, up to 12,400 dollars. That's 1,240 dollars of tax.
The rest spills into the 12 percent bucket: 26,500 dollars, taxed at 12 percent, is 3,180 dollars. Add them up: 4,420 dollars for the year.
Your marginal rate is the rate on your next dollar: 12 percent. Your effective rate is your total tax divided by your income: 4,420 over 55,000, about 8 percent.
That's why a raise never lowers your take-home pay. If a raise reaches the 22 percent bucket, only the new dollars pay 22 percent. Everything below keeps its lower rate.
Your W-4 tells your employer how much to withhold from each check. With one job, fill in Steps 1 and 5. With two jobs, check the box in Step 2.
In April, you compare. If more was withheld than you owed, you get a refund: your own money back. If less was withheld, you owe the difference.
Think of rice terraces on a hillside. Water fills the top terrace, then spills to the next. Filling a lower step never empties the ones above. Brackets work the same way.
